title: CBA staff stand-off ends with 13pc pay rise deal
full_text:
Commonwealth Bank has ended months of terse union negotiations with an agreement that guarantees 35,000 employees pay rises over three years and establishes an artificial intelligence committee to help staff cope with the changes brought on by the technology.
The Finance Sector Union confirmed it had come to an in-principle agreement with Australia's largest bank and its Bankwest subsidiary on Tuesday after securing a series of hard-won concessions, including a guaranteed 13 per cent pay rise over three years for its lowest-paid staff.
The new enterprise bargaining agreement promises staggered raises across the 2027, 2028 and 2029 financial years, with the size of the increase to be determined by four employee pay bands, which will be now indexed to rise with inflation.
Packaged employees, typically made up of managers and corporate office workers, earning less than $103,500 will receive 12 per cent over the three-year period.
Those making between $103,500 and $126,000 will secure a 9.5 per cent bump, between $126,000 and $165,000 will gain 7.25 per cent, and anyone on more than $165,000 will see their pay go up 5 per cent.
Unpackaged employees, typically frontline and lower- to middle-tier staff such as bank tellers, will receive slightly higher percentage increases, with each of those bands securing 13, 11, 10 and 6.5 per cent respectively.
CBA has agreed to simplify performance-related pay, increasing discretionary bonuses available to high-performing staff. Workers have also won an additional two weeks of paid parental leave, taking them to a 20-week entitlement, as well as five days of paid reproductive leave.
The agreement, which will now be voted on by workers, ends a six-month stand-off between the union and management, during which the FSU weaponised chief executive Matt Comyn's $9.1 million pay packet in support of its campaign.
The deal comes the day before the board is scheduled to face shareholders at its annual general meeting, avoiding the prospect of an ugly protest.
The EBA negotiations have been among the most protracted in the financial sector in recent memory, topped only by the ongoing dispute between the Reserve Bank of Australia and its workforce, which has now boiled over to the Fair Work Commission.
With bank workers increasingly anxious at the prospect of burgeoning AI use, the bank agreed to establish an AI committee as well as a provision supporting workforce change.
"The proposed enterprise agreement includes a new AI Committee to support ongoing dialogue with employees and the FSU about AI-enabled change, workforce trends and opportunities for training, capability development and reskilling," a CBA spokesman said.
Last year, CBA replaced dozens of call centre workers with AI before swiftly backtracking and reinstating their jobs. Appearing last week at parliamentary committee hearing on AI, Comyn acknowledged it was a mistake and apologised again for it.
The FSU claimed the deal as a major victory and one that sets a strong starting point for negotiations with the other big four banks over the coming year.
FSU acting national secretary Nicole McPherson said the 13 per cent raise for the bank's lowest-paid staff ranked as the highest pay bump in the sector.
"CBA's previous below-inflation pay offers were insulting to workers and only motivated them to demand a fairer share of the profits they helped to create," McPherson said. "The FSU congratulates our members for standing up and exposing conditions at Australia's richest bank."
The union is already in negotiations with National Australia Bank with its enterprise bargaining agreement due to expire on December 31, followed by ANZ's in September and Westpac's at the end of 2027.
The Commonwealth Bank posted an $11 billion full-year profit in August, up 7 per cent on the previous year, but its shares have struggled this year - down around 4 per cent so far - amid investor concerns its market valuation had run too far ahead of fundamentals.
